title: OpenAI partners with Chile's government to train civil servants on AI and support local startups
summary: If you work in Chile's public sector and want to use AI tools safely, or run a startup that wants to build with OpenAI, this partnership could matter to you. OpenAI has announced a collaboration with the government of Chile focused on responsible adoption in the public sector, skills training for civil servants, and support for the local startup ecosystem.
ai_summary: On November 17, 2026, OpenAI announced a partnership with the government of Chile, launching "OpenAI for Chile" led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation. The collaboration focuses on responsible AI adoption in the public sector, AI literacy and skills training for civil servants, and helping local startups access OpenAI programs and technology. Planned activities may include workshops, train-the-trainer sessions, technical guidance and mentorship, and could connect public institutions with universities. The memorandum of understanding includes no investment or purchasing commitments; specific activities, resources and technology access will be agreed separately, subject to privacy, information security and responsible-use safeguards. For Chilean civil servants and founders, it offers access to tools, training and networks—what they ultimately get depends on priorities set by the joint task force.
brief: The partnership was announced on November 17, 2026. It is led by Chile's Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, with Minister Ximena Lincolao signing the MoU on Chile's behalf.
The MoU explicitly includes no investment or purchasing commitments. Specific activities, eligibility and technology access will be agreed separately.
Civil servant training plans mention workshops and a train-the-trainer approach, covering checking AI outputs, protecting sensitive information and maintaining human oversight.
Startups could gain access to OpenAI programs and technology, technical guidance and mentorship, along with opportunities to connect with public institutions and universities.

blocks.p: "OpenAI for Chile" is a government partnership announced by OpenAI on November 17, 2026 and led by Chile's Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation. Its goals are to bring AI into public administration, build civil servants' skills, and help local startups create useful applications.

It is not a product launch but a memorandum of understanding (MoU), a framework document that signals intent to cooperate without committing to payment or purchases. The MoU was signed on the sidelines of Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, with Minister Ximena Lincolao signing for Chile.

The partnership builds on Chile's National AI Policy and action plan, which already support talent development, research and responsible adoption. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in the announcement that he looks forward to helping Chilean civil servants use these tools, improve public services, and support entrepreneurs starting new companies.

sections.h: How does it fit with Chile's own AI plans?

blocks.p: Chile already has its own National AI Policy and action plan, focused on talent development, research and responsible adoption. Rather than imposing a separate program, OpenAI is building this partnership on Chile's existing policy framework so it aligns more closely with local priorities.

The partnership is also supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce's American SI Exports Program, an export support initiative in which OpenAI is an anchor partner. In practice, OpenAI as a U.S. company is helping Chile advance its own AI goals through an official export-support program, specifically in public sector innovation, skills development and entrepreneurship.

For civil servants, the partnership is built around practical AI literacy, including upskilling and reskilling tailored to specific roles. The announcement says the partners will "explore" this and that activities "could include" these elements, so they are directions under consideration rather than a finalized curriculum.

list: Workshops: teaching how to use AI tools effectively.
Train-the-trainer: teaching one group first so they can train more colleagues.
Checking outputs: learning to review AI-generated results instead of accepting them at face value.
Protecting sensitive information: civil servants handle private material, so they need to learn not to feed sensitive data into tools carelessly.
Maintaining human oversight: AI supports the work, but humans still make the final decisions and carry the responsibility.

blocks.p: For Chilean AI startups, the focus is access: the partners will explore how founders can get relevant OpenAI programs and technology, as well as practical learning, technical guidance and mentorship.

Another focus is connections: the partnership could link entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and local partners to build applications that support Chile's economic development and public-service priorities. In other words, it is not just about tools but also about networks and real-world settings.
The announcement also makes clear that which companies are eligible and what resources they receive will be agreed separately later; there is no application process right now.

sections.h: How will the public sector itself use AI?

blocks.p: Beyond training others, the ministry itself plans to pilot AI: the partnership will explore adopting AI technology in its administrative processes, including potential support from OpenAI on adopting new models, plus advice and training for ministry staff.
This part is also framed with "explore" and "potential," so it is still at the stage of figuring out where and how AI could be used, not a system that has already been deployed.

sections.h: Who drives it, and how will it be implemented?

blocks.p: Implementation won't happen automatically once the agreement is signed. The announcement says a joint task force of representatives from Chile's science ministry and OpenAI will first agree on priorities and an initial workplan, then set leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity.

steps.name: Form a joint task force

steps.desc: Set leads, milestones and measures of success.

steps.name: Implement

list: Money: The MoU includes no investment or purchasing commitments. The two sides have not discussed specific amounts, and the document does not trigger any spending.
Timeline: The task force has not yet agreed priorities or an initial workplan, so the announcement does not say when training will start or how long pilots will run.
Specific models: The announcement only says OpenAI may support "adopting new models"; it does not say which models, how they would be deployed, or whether that means cloud or on-premises.
Startup eligibility and limits: Whether access is free, how many spots exist, and what pricing applies will all be agreed separately later.
Training scale: The announcement does not say how many civil servants will take part or which departments are covered.
Data and privacy specifics: It only says activities will be subject to safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use, without giving a concrete plan.

blocks.p: The partnership's value is in the potential: civil servants could get practical AI training, startups could get technology and mentorship, and the science ministry could speed up modernization of its administrative processes. For Chile's local ecosystem, it's a chance to connect to international AI capability.

The limitations and barriers are also clear: there is no money, no confirmed product, and no confirmed timeline right now. All concrete benefits must wait for the joint task force, and they come with privacy and information-security constraints. In other words, don't treat this as an immediate benefit you can use.

list: If you work in Chile's government or public sector: watch whether your department joins a training pilot later, and keep an eye on official channels for the workplan.
If you're building an AI startup in Chile: learn about OpenAI for Countries and related startup programs now, and evaluate whether they fit once eligibility and resource terms are published.

If you're just following OpenAI's global government partnerships: this is another step under OpenAI for Countries, and the page also lists its earlier work across US government levels and its skills partnership with Grab in Southeast Asia.
